detail:
NIAMS describes psoriatic arthritis as a form of arthritis, or joint inflammation, that can occur in people who have psoriasis, the skin disease that causes scaly, inflamed patches. It is an immune-mediated condition: the immune system drives inflammation in both skin and joints, and researchers believe genes and environmental factors both contribute. Joint disease may appear years after the skin disease, at the same time, or occasionally first.

Symptoms can include joint pain, swelling, and stiffness that may come and go, tenderness where tendons and ligaments attach to bone, especially the heel and the bottom of the foot, painful sausage-like swelling of a whole finger or toe, and inflammation of the spine causing back pain and stiffness. Skin and nail changes, such as pitting or crumbling nails, and fatigue can accompany the joint symptoms, and eye inflammation occurs in some people. NIAMS notes there is no single test: clinicians usually rely on the history of psoriasis, a joint and skin examination, imaging, and blood tests used in part to rule out conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and gout.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about joint symptoms in psoriasis.
sourceName: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
summary: NIAMS describes psoriatic arthritis as immune-driven joint inflammation occurring in people with psoriasis, with symptoms that can include swollen, stiff joints, heel tenderness, sausage-like digits, and nail changes, diagnosed clinically rather than by a single test.
takeaways: psoriatic arthritis links skin psoriasis with joint inflammation
symptoms can include swollen joints and sausage-like digits
heel and tendon attachment pain is a characteristic feature
no single test confirms it; exam and history lead
title: Psoriatic arthritis: when psoriasis reaches the joints
